blocks.text: The Polish conditional covers English “would”, “could” and “if I were.” It does three jobs: it makes requests polite (*Czy mógłbyś…?*), it presents something as hypothetical (*Poszłabym, ale…*), and, with *gdyby*, it builds unreal conditions (*Gdybyś chciała, poszlibyśmy*).
How it’s built
Start from the past form without its person marker, the l-participle, then add the particle *by* and the person marker. Ania’s *poszłabym*, “I would go”:

So the conditional shares everything with the past tense: the same stems, the same gender and number agreement, the same virile *-li* and non-virile *-ły*. One difference: the masculine has no inserted *e*, because *by* now stands between *ł* and the marker: *byłem* in the past, but *byłbym* in the conditional.
The full paradigm
Any verb works the same way once you know its past stem: *chciałbym*, *mogłabyś*, *pojechalibyśmy*, *zrobiłoby*. The third person has no marker: *byłoby*, “it would be.”
A particle that moves
*By* and its person marker can leave the verb and attach to an earlier word in the clause, usually the first one. This is fully standard, not just colloquial:

items.en: I’d be the one to forget.

blocks.text: It’s especially common after question words and pronouns. Spelling follows the position: joined to the verb (*poszłabym*), written as a separate word everywhere else (*ja bym*, *co byś*).
Politeness
Requests and wishes sound abrupt in the plain present, so Polish speakers reach for the conditional:
If-clauses: gdyby and jeśli
For unreal or hypothetical conditions, Polish uses *gdyby* in the if-clause and the conditional in the main clause. The person marker attaches to *gdyby*, and the verb stays a bare past form:

items.en: If you wanted to, we could go together.

items.pl: Gdybym zdała egzamin, pojechalibyśmy nad morze.
items.en: If I passed the test, we’d drive to the seaside.

blocks.text: Never put the marker on the verb as well: *gdybyś chciała*, not *gdybyś chciałaś* or *gdyby chciałaś*.

For real, open conditions, use *jeśli* or *jeżeli* with ordinary tenses: *Jeśli będę miał czas, przyjdę*, “If I have time, I’ll come.” The choice between *jeśli* and *gdyby* is the choice between a real possibility and an imagined one.
Present or past?

Polish has one conditional for all times. *Gdybym wiedział, przyszedłbym* means both “If I knew, I’d come” and “If I had known, I would have come”; context decides. A compound past conditional (*byłbym przyszedł*) exists, but it’s literary and rarely heard.
Żeby: wanting someone else to act

*Żeby* (also *aby*) works like *gdyby*: it carries the person marker and takes a bare past form. After verbs of wanting, asking and so on, it introduces a clause whose subject differs from the main clause:
If the subject is the same, use the infinitive instead: *Chcę przyjść*, “I want to come.”
